How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Interpersonal contact is essential for cooperation and care, but it also provides a route for pathogen transmission between individuals. Hence, a key challenge for social organisms involves maintaining beneficial social contact while also limiting exposure to infection risks. Existing proposals suggest that this trade-off is guided by the interpersonal value of specific social targets. In addition, ecological and cultural factors including historical pathogen prevalence, individualismcollectivism, tightness-looseness, and relational mobility might also shape how people avoid pathogens. To test whether and how infection-risky social contact varies with individual-level interpersonal value and these societal-level factors, we collected data from 61 societies (n = 42,756). Participants were randomly assigned to imagine targets who varied in interpersonal value, then rated their comfort with infection-risky contact with that target (e.g., drinking from the same water bottle) and whether they would touch the target when greeting them. In all societies, participants were more comfortable with infection-risky contact and more likely to engage in physical contact during greetings with targets of higher interpersonal value. Such associations varied only modestly across societies. Notably, the associations between infection-risky contact and societal-level factors depended on target interpersonal value and were concentrated among high-value targets -contact was lower where historical pathogen prevalence and tightness were greater, and higher where individualism and relational mobility were greater. These findings suggest that infection-risky contact is primarily guided by the value of social targets, with ecological and cultural factors playing a lesser role.

Balancing the benefits of social contact against infection risks is a fundamental challenge faced throughout human evolution. Prior work proposes that this trade-off is embedded in mental processes that track the interpersonal value of social partners. If this account is correct, the link between interpersonal value and infection-risky contact should be universal. We find that it is: across 61 societies, people were consistently more willing to engage in infection-risky contact with high-value social partners. Diverse societal-level factors also related to infection-risky contact, but specifically for high-value targets rather than low-value ones. Findings support the universality of a social psychology of pathogen avoidance that considers the interpersonal value of targets while also being calibrated by societal factors.

Main Text Introduction

Across species, pathogens have driven the evolution of myriad adaptations that function to mitigate infection risks (1). In humans, such adaptations include psychological mechanisms that detect illness cues in others (e.g., skin lesions, lethargy, pallor) and subsequently motivate avoidance of those possessing such cues (2). Nevertheless, infected individuals sometimes do not produce detectable symptoms (2, 3). Further, even people who are not themselves infected can transmit any pathogens that might be present on their hands. Minimizing contact even with seemingly healthy others reduces the likelihood of infection, but completely avoiding infectionrisky contact is not feasible. After all, everyday interactions -including sharing food, exchanging objects, and providing or receiving care -are essential for social life. Consequently, people must weigh the social benefits of contact with others against the corresponding infection risks of proximity, indirect contact (i.e., touching things that another person has touched), and direct contact (i.e., touching another person's body). In sum, the challenge of maintaining beneficial contact while limiting exposure to infectious microbes is one that humans have had to navigate across all epochs and all ecologies (4, 5).

The recurring nature of this challenge suggests that humans may possess dedicated mental processes that regulate infection-risky contact by balancing infection costs against social benefits.

A similar cost-benefit logic underlies other adaptive decisions. For instance, foraging decisions involve weighing nutritional and energetic returns against the time, energy, and predation risks required to obtain food (5, 6). Social interactions are structured similarly: people assign weight to other people's welfare relative to their own, and they preferentially allocate benefits to those they value more relative to those they value less (4, 5, 7). Valuation processes have been proposed to integrate multiple features of an individual, including genetic relatedness, ability and likelihood to reciprocate, and formidability, into a welfare trade-off ratio (WTR) -a mental representation of interpersonal value (5, 8, 9). Evidence from both industrialized and forager societies is consistent with the existence of such a process: WTR relates to a number of emotions and behaviors relevant to valuation, including helping, cooperation, gratitude, and forgiveness (5, 7, 8, 10, 11). In addition, preliminary findings in a few populations suggest that interpersonal value might also relate to behaviors not typically considered in the cooperation literature -those relevant to pathogen transmission. For example, mothers report less disgust toward their own infants' diapers than toward those of unrelated infants (12), foragers provide more care to those sick individuals who are expected to reciprocate (13, 14), and U.S. and Dutch participants are more comfortable engaging in interpersonal contact that risks microbe transmission (e.g., using the same towel) with people they value more than with people they value less (9, 15). If natural selection shaped mechanisms that use valuation to regulate pathogen avoidance, then the link between interpersonal value and infection-risky social contact should be universal across populations.

This proposal of a universal relation between interpersonal value and infection-risky social contact is distinct from a body of work proposing that human pathogen avoidance varies markedly across societies as a function of a specific ecological variable: historical pathogen prevalence. Findings in this area suggest that higher historical pathogen prevalence is associated with lower extraversion, less romantic kissing, and greater racial prejudice (16) (17) (18) (19). These findings, however, face two notable challenges. First, many outcome variables (e.g., extraversion) examined in the literature have ambiguous consequences for infection risk. Second, the reported relations between pathogen prevalence and outcome variables are often not robust to corrections for societal non-independence (20, 21). Given these challenges, the relation between ecological pathogen prevalence and behaviors with clear consequences for infectious disease remains unclear. Parasite-stress theory nonetheless makes a straightforward prediction: infection-risky contact should be lower overall in societies with higher pathogen prevalence.

Parasite-stress theory also implies that pathogen prevalence might shape the relation between interpersonal value and infection-risky contact. It proposes that higher pathogen prevalence is associated with the tendency to interact more with high-value others such as friends and kin and less with low-value others such as strangers and outgroup members (17, 22, 23). Whereas existing work has examined covariation between societal-level pathogen prevalence and collectivism, family ties, and racial prejudice, none has tested whether pathogen prevalence differentially relates to willingness to engage in infection-risky contact with social partners differing on interpersonal value. Following parasite stress theory, the relation between interpersonal value and infection-risky contact should be stronger in societies with high pathogen prevalence than those with low pathogen prevalence. Specifically, pathogen prevalence should constrain contact with low-value targets more than with high-value ones.

In addition to ecological history, multiple cultural factors might also relate to infection-risky social contact (24) (25) (26). Tighter cultures, which emphasize adherence to norms and punishment of deviance (31), experienced fewer cases and deaths during the early period of the COVID-19 pandemic (32). Conversely, societies with greater relational mobility -the tendency to freely choose and replace social partners like friends (27) -experienced faster spread of COVID-19 (28). Collectivist values also might shape patterns of infection-risky contact by encouraging interactions with close others over those with distant others (29, 30). As with ecological pathogen prevalence, though, evidence for relations between cultural factors and infection-risky social contact is limited and indirect, and no work speaks to whether these same factors might moderate how interpersonal value relates to such contact.

Empirical investigation

We collected data from 42,756 participants across 61 societies. Each participant was asked to imagine a specific social target. To guarantee variation in the interpersonal value of those targets, we randomly assigned participants to think of a target from one of four folk relationship categories: their closest friend, an acquaintance, a stranger, or a person they know personally and dislike intensely (hereafter enemy). They completed a welfare trade-off task with this person in mind; results from this task were used to estimate WTR, with a greater value indicating that the participant values the target's financial welfare more. They then reported (i) their comfort with a set of everyday actions that risk exposure to the target's microbes through close physical proximity or contact with the same objects, such as sitting close enough that one's leg touches the target's or drinking from the same water bottle as the target (hereafter contact comfort); and (ii) their likelihood of physically touching the target during greetings, such as with handshakes, hugs, or kisses (hereafter contact greeting).

Using these data, the present study (i) assessed cross-societal variation in contact comfort and contact greeting; (ii) tested whether the relation between interpersonal value and these behaviors is universal across societies; (iii) examined how historical pathogen prevalence and cultural factors relate to these behaviors; and (iv) evaluated whether historical pathogen prevalence or cultural factors moderate any relation between interpersonal value and these behaviors. Analyses were first conducted using frequentist multilevel models. Results of these analyses are reported with parameter estimates, 95% confidence intervals (CI), and p-values. To evaluate robustness, key findings were reexamined using Bayesian multilevel models accounting for societal nonindependence (see Data Analysis); these results are reported with posterior medians and 95% credible intervals (CrI). In the main text, we mainly focus on relations between WTR and the dependent measures. Detailed results concerning relationship categories are reported in the SI (Sections S3.3 to S3.7).

Results

Does infection-risky social contact vary across societies?

Contact comfort varied little across societies: about 3% of the total variance was explained by between-society differences (ICC = 0.03). Contact greeting diverged more, with 7% of variance explained by societal differences (latent ICC = 0.07). Figure 1 shows the society-level random intercepts for contact comfort and contact greeting, representing deviations from the grand mean. For context, a different study of 21 psychological variables measured across 69 societies revealed ICCs ranging from 0.03 to 0.28, with a median of 0.10 (33). Hence, cross-societal variation in contact comfort is among the lowest within this wide array of variables, whereas variation in contact greeting falls near the middle of the distribution. predicted means (A) or probabilities (B) derived from the random intercepts of intercept-only multilevel models. Error bars indicate approximate 95% uncertainty intervals (±1.96 posterior standard deviations) around the society-specific intercept estimates. Vertical dashed lines denote the grand mean (A) and the grand predicted probability (B) across societies.

Is infection-risky social contact positively associated with interpersonal value across societies?

As shown in the left panel of Figure 2, correlations between WTR and both contact comfort and contact greeting were positive within every society (all ps < 0.05; Table S4). Meta-analyses of within-society correlations yielded average correlations of r = 0.43 (95% CI [0.42, 0.45], p < 0.001) for contact comfort and r = 0.25 (95% CI [0.24, 0.27], p < 0.001) for contact greeting, with limited between-society heterogeneity in both associations (contact comfort: 𝜏2 = 0.003; contact greeting: 𝜏2 = 0.002). Across societies, the associations between WTR and both outcomes remained statistically significant when accounting for relationship category (contact comfort: b = 0.76, 95% CI [0.71, 0.80], p < 0.001; contact greeting: OR = 1.84, 95% CI [1.73, 1.95], p < 0.001). Models accounting for societal non-independence also showed positive associations (contact comfort: bMedian = 0.75, 95% CrI [0.71, 0.80]; contact greeting: ORMedian = 1.84, 95% CrI [1.73, 1.95]). Taken together, results indicated that higher interpersonal value consistently related to greater willingness to engage in infection-risky contact across societies, and that this relation remained even within relationship categories.

Is infection-risk social contact lower in societies with higher pathogen prevalence?

The association between contact comfort and pathogen prevalence was statistically significant (b = -0.12, 95% CI [-0.21, -0.03], p < 0.01, semi-partial R² = 0.006). Further accounting for societal non-independence yielded a 95% credible interval that included zero (bMedian = -0.08, 95% CrI [-0.20, 0.04]). The relation between contact greeting and pathogen prevalence was nonsignificant (OR = 1.18, 95% CI [0.94, 1.49], p = 0.168, semi-partial R² = 0.0005). In sum, results did not support a general association between pathogen prevalence and infection-risky contact.

Is infection-risky social contact related to cultural factors?

Relations between contact comfort and both relational mobility (b = 0.13, 95% CI [0.06, 0.21], p < 0.001, semi-partial R² = 0.03) and individualism (b = 0.10, 95% CI [0.04, 0.16], p < 0.001, semipartial R² = 0.01) were statistically significant. Models accounting for societal non-independence showed that the 95% credible interval for individualism included zero (bMedian = 0.06, 95% CrI [-0.02, 0.14]), whereas that for relational mobility excluded zero (bMedian = 0.11, 95% CrI [0.01, 0.21]). The relation between tightness-looseness and contact comfort was not statistically significant (b = -0.02, 95% CI [-0.08, 0.05], p = 0.638, semi-partial R² = 0.01).

For contact greeting, the relation with relational mobility was statistically significant (OR = 1.43, 95% CI [1.16, 1.77], p < 0.001, semi-partial R² = 0.03), but accounting for societal non-independence yielded a 95% credible interval that included 1 (ORMedian = 1.21, 95% CrI [0.98, 1.48]). Relations between pathogen prevalence and both individualism (OR = 0.92, 95% CI [0.77, 1.11], p = 0.39, semi-partial R² = 0.005) and tightness-looseness (OR = 0.86, 95% CI [0.73, 1.03], p = 0.1, semipartial R² = 0.005) were nonsignificant. In sum, as with pathogen prevalence, results did not support general associations between infection-risky contact and the cultural factors tested here, with only the relation between contact comfort and relational mobility being robust.

Is the relation between interpersonal value and infection-risky social contact moderated by pathogen prevalence and cultural factors?

The interaction between pathogen prevalence and WTR was statistically significant for both contact comfort (b = -0.11, 95% CI [-0.18, -0.04], p = 0.002) and contact greeting (OR = 0.82, 95% CI [0.75, 0.89], p < 0.001), and these interactions were robust in models accounting for societal nonindependence (contact comfort: bMedian = -0.11, 95% CrI [-0.18, -0.04]; contact greeting: ORMedian = 0.82, 95% CrI [0.75, 0.90]). Contrary to predictions, simple slope analyses indicated that the association between WTR and contact comfort was slightly stronger in societies with lower pathogen prevalence (e.g., b = 1.21 at -1 SD) than in those with higher pathogen prevalence (e.g., b = 1.06 at +1 SD), as was the relation between WTR and contact greeting (OR = 3.06 versus OR = 2.29; details are shown in Figures 3A and B).

Simple slope analyses examining the relations between pathogen prevalence and contact comfort for high-versus low-value targets were also inconsistent with predictions. As shown in Figure 3C, for relatively high-value targets (e.g., WTR at 1.55 and 1), contact comfort decreased as pathogen prevalence increased (ps < 0.001 and 95% credible intervals excluded zero); for low-value targets (e.g., WTR at -0.45 and 0), the relation between contact comfort and pathogen prevalence was not robust (ps > 0.05 or 95% credible intervals included zero). Results examining how pathogen prevalence related to contact comfort within relationship categories rather than WTR indicated a similar pattern (Section S3.5): the relation was negative within relatively high-value relationships (e.g., friends and acquaintances), but was not robust for low-value relationships (e.g., strangers or enemies). Simple slopes of pathogen prevalence on contact greeting were not robust when accounting for societal non-independence at any of the tested levels of WTR (Figure 3D) or within any relationship category (Section S3.5).

Cultural factors also moderated the association between interpersonal value and infection-risky contact. The interaction between WTR and individualism was statistically significant for both outcomes (contact comfort: b = 0.08, 95% CI [0.03, 0.13], p = 0.002; contact greeting: OR = 1.17, 95% CI [1.10, 1.24], p < 0.001), and remained robust in models accounting for societal nonindependence (contact comfort: bMedian = 0.08, 95% CrI [0.03, 0.14]; contact greeting: ORMedian = 1.16, 95% CrI [1.09, 1 .25]). The interaction between WTR and tightness was statistically significant for contact comfort (b = -0.07, 95% CI [-0.13, -0.01], p = 0.019), but not for contact greeting (OR = 0.94, 95% CI [0.88, 1.00], p = 0.069). The former remained robust in models accounting for societal non-independence (bMedian = -0.09, 95% CrI [-0.17, -0.01]). The interaction between WTR and relational mobility was statistically significant for both outcomes (contact comfort: b = 0.08, 95% CI [ 0.02, 0.14], p = 0.01; contact greeting: OR = 1.09, 95% CI [1.01, 1.18], p = 0.023), and both remained robust in models accounting for societal non-independence (contact comfort: bMedian = 0.08, 95% CrI [0.01, 0.14]; contact greeting: ORMedian = 1.09, 95% CrI [1.01, 1.19]). Simple slope analyses showed that the positive association between WTR and infection-risky contact strengthened as individualism and relational mobility increased but weakened as tightness increased, though these differences in slope magnitude were modest (Figure S1). Similar to pathogen prevalence, cultural moderations on infection-risky contact were primarily observed among relatively high-value targets, whereas moderation for low-value targets was not robust (Figure S2). A similar pattern emerged when examining relationship categories instead of WTR, with robust association between cultural factors and infection-risky contact primarily observed for relatively high-value relationships (Section S3.6).

Discussion

Across all cultures and times, humans must balance the infection costs against the social benefits of interpersonal contact. Given the ambiguity of infection status in others, a well-designed system for regulating infection risks should not rely on pathogen cues alone, but should also incorporate other types of social information (4, 5). In all 61 societies sampled, participants were more comfortable engaging in infection-risky contact with -and more likely to touch when greetingsocial partners whose welfare they valued more. There was little variability in the magnitude of these relations. Such consistency across wide and diverse societies suggests a broadly shared psychology in which the interpersonal value of a social partner guides motivations to embrace or avoid infection-risky contact.

The cross-societal breadth of the study afforded a novel test of parasite stress theory, which suggests that individuals in high pathogen prevalence societies should invest more in avoiding infection risks, especially those posed by targets lower in interpersonal value. Contrary to these predictions, results did not reveal a general relation between pathogen prevalence and infectionrisky contact. However, they did indicate that pathogen prevalence is associated with lower contact comfort specifically with high-value targets (i.e., those with high WTR or those considered friends) rather than low-value ones (i.e., those with low WTR or those considered strangers or enemies). Although these results are not straightforwardly consistent with predictions from parasite stress theory, which emphasizes greater contact avoidance with strangers and outgroup members in high pathogen-prevalence societies, they are interpretable under the framework presented here. Given that contact with low-value others offers little social benefit, there is little to gain from contact that could transmit pathogens, even when the pathogen ecology is relatively benign. Because potential benefits are substantial for high-value targets, infection risk is more relevant for decisions to embrace or reject contact. Consequently, people accept that risk more readily where pathogen prevalence is low than where it is high.

Similar patterns emerged for the three cultural factors examined here -relational mobility, individualism-collectivism, and tightness-looseness. As with pathogen prevalence, each related to infection-risky social contact with high-value targets but not low-value ones. Each of these variables reflects a more flexible, less constrained social environment, with consequences for how relationships are formed, maintained, and dissolved (30, 34, 35). Cultural variation of this kind has been proposed to arise partially in response to ecological threats, including those posed by pathogens (32, 36, 37). Consistent with this view, evidence suggests that such cultural factors relate to the acceptance of anti-pathogen innovations (e.g., mask usage) and to the spread of some diseases (28, 32, 38). The current results suggest that they might also influence how people weigh the costs and benefits of social contact with high-value targets. When relationships are relatively more flexible and easier to dissolve, maintaining valued relationships demands greater investment. Given that infection-risky behaviors (e.g., saliva sharing) can indicate relational closeness (39, 40), tolerating the risks of such acts might be more beneficial in such societies. Similarly, when societies place fewer normative constraints on behaviors, as in relatively loose ones (31), individuals might feel freer to capitalize on the benefits of contact, such as showing the willingness to tolerate infection risks to express closeness to valued targets.

Overall, pathogen prevalence, individualism-collectivism, relational mobility, and tightnesslooseness each related to infection-risky social contact for high-value targets but not low-value ones. The similarity in these patterns highlights the challenge of attributing cross-societal relations to any single factor, especially since they are correlated. Instead, the findings imply a common tradeoff: balancing the social benefits of contact with valued others against potential infection costs. And, indeed, despite modest differences in the slope of the relation between interpersonal value and contact variables across society-level variables, that relation was robust and positive in every society assessed, regardless of pathogen prevalence or cultural variables.

Notably, societal variation in contact greeting was larger than societal variation in contact comfort. Unlike the latter, which reflects internal motivations to engage in everyday actions that might incidentally carry pathogen transmission risks, greetings are ritualized actions that communicate information not only to the partner but also to observers. Such actions can signal cooperative intent, relative status, likelihood to aggress, and knowledge of and adherence to social norms, and their meaning can vary across societies (41) (42) (43) (44). For example, a study found that bowing in Japan increases the perceived attractiveness of the bower, but does not do so in other East Asian cultures or other cultural contexts (45). The larger variation in greeting behaviors likely reflects additional differences in social signaling conventions rather than a greater difference between societies in the trade-off that regulates infection-risky social contact.

To ensure variation in WTR within societies and to prevent cross-societal variation in WTR emerging from cross-societal differences in the types of targets participants reported on, we randomly assigned participants to report on a target belonging to one of four folk relationship categories: their closest friend, an acquaintance, a stranger, or an enemy. While WTR accounted for variance in contact comfort and contact greeting even within relationship categories, relationship category also accounted for variance in both measures independent of WTR (Tables S6 and S10). We offer two explanations for this outcome. First, the brief welfare-tradeoff task used here is an imperfect measure of WTR. Measurement error would attenuate the estimated effect of WTR and, consequently, inflate variance attributed uniquely to relationship category, which is correlated with true WTR. Second, relationship category and WTR each carry information the other does not. Category labels such as "friend" connote relational history and expected benefits beyond the welfare weighting that WTR captures, while WTR reflects willingness to sacrifice financially for reasons that a category label might not, such as formidability (7). These explanations are not mutually exclusive: some of the unique effects of folk relationship category might result from measurement issues; others might reflect relational information that is distinct from WTR.

Hypotheses were generated from an adaptationist approach to cognitive science, which proposes that humans possess computational processes specialized for navigating recurrent adaptive problems, including those involving pathogen risk and cooperation (4, 5, 46). The present findings are consistent with this view, but they do not speak to the degree of specialization underlying the relation between interpersonal value and infection-risky contact. The same relation could potentially emerge from mechanisms that are not specialized for pathogen avoidance per se, but draw upon culturally-transmitted knowledge, such as that grounded in germ theory. This possibility is difficult to exclude given that the sample included only individuals with internet access and 21 st -century educational backgrounds. Two lines of evidence nonetheless speak against this possibility: people in the kinds of small-scale societies that humans evolved in appear to compute welfare tradeoffs much as people in societies with widespread internet access do (8), and people without formal education or knowledge of germ theory still possess a psychology of contamination (47, 48). Even so, future work could verify that relations observed in the populations sampled here are also apparent in small-scale societies less exposed to such culturally-transmitted knowledge.

In conclusion, the present work demonstrates that the value people place on their social partners has implications beyond cooperation and other prosocial behaviors: it also relates to their willingness to expose themselves to potentially infectious microbes transmitted by another person. The relation between interpersonal value and infection-risky contact appears consistently across societies, though its magnitude shows some variation across social and ecological conditions. These findings reveal a potentially universal aspect of human psychology whose expression bends to local contexts.

Materials and Methods

This project was approved by the Scientific and Ethical Review Board (VCWE) of the Faculty of Behavioural and Movement Sciences, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. Participants completed an online survey on interpersonal value and willingness to engage in infection-risky social contact, and all provided informed consent at the beginning of the survey. After providing demographic information, participants were randomly assigned to imagine one of four types of social targets: their closest friend, an acquaintance, a stranger, or a person they disliked intensely. Further instructions on target assignment are provided in SI Appendix. The target was referred to as Person X in subsequent measures.

Interpersonal value.

Interpersonal value was assessed using a decision-making task that estimated participants' welfare trade-off ratio (WTR) toward Person X (8). On each trial, participants chose between a self-benefiting option (the participant received money and the target received nothing) and a target-benefiting option (the target received money and the participant received nothing). Across trials, the amount benefiting the participant varied, while the amount benefiting the target remained fixed. WTR was estimated as the point at which participants switched their preference from the self-benefiting option to the target-benefiting option, reflecting the relative value they placed on the target's welfare compared to their own. Details of the task procedure and calculation of WTR are reported in SI Appendix. Greater WTR reflects placing greater value on others' welfare relative to one's own. Contact comfort. Participants rated their comfort with contact with Person X across five infection-risky behaviors on a 7-point Likert scale (from1 = very uncomfortable to7 = very comfortable). These behaviors included, for example, "sitting close enough to Person X that your legs are touching", "standing close enough to Person X that his/her saliva might splash onto your face", and "drinking from the same water bottle as Person X". Evidence supporting the reliability and validity of this measure is provided in SI Appendix. Higher scores indicate greater comfort with these behaviors.

Contact greeting.

Participants also reported whether they would physically touch Person X during a typical greeting (e.g., handshaking, hugging, or kissing; coded as0 = No and1 = Yes). Higher value indicates a higher likelihood of physical contact during greetings.

Societal-level factors. Societal-level factors -including historical pathogen prevalence of nine diseases (e.g., tuberculosis) (47) and cultural indices of individualism-collectivism (30), tightnesslooseness (31, 32), and relational mobility (35) -were obtained from existing studies.

Data analysis.

We examined within-society associations between interpersonal value and both contact comfort and contact greeting by estimating Pearson correlations between WTR and both outcomes (reporting two-tailed p-values) for each society, and then assessing the heterogeneity of these associations across societies using meta-analyses. We tested the between-society variation in contact comfort and contact greeting using the intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) from intercept-only models with participants nested within societies. Then, using linear multilevel models, we analyzed the associations of contact comfort with both interpersonal value and societal-level factors. Contact greeting was analyzed analogously using multilevel logistic regression models. To account for non-independence among societies, we fit Bayesian multilevel models with structured random effects in which the covariance was determined by a Gaussian process based on geographic locations and/or a linguistic similarity matrix (21). Further details regarding the methods and analyses are reported in SI Appendix. 46. L. Cosmides, J. Tooby, Evolutionary Psychology: New Perspectives on Cognition and Motivation. Annu. Rev. Materials and methods S1.1. Participants This project was approved by the Scientific and Ethical Review Board (VCWE) of the Faculty of Behavioural and Movement Sciences, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam (approval VCWE-2023-023).

All participants provided informed consent at the beginning of the survey.

Participants were recruited via two routes: (i) a panel research company (Cint) and (ii) university samples (mostly undergraduate students). As of June 27, 2025, a total of 50,594 panel participants and 32,553 university participants accessed the online survey. Of these, 47,564 participants provided complete responses. From this group, we excluded testing data (collaborators' testing responses in the university sample), underage respondents, and inattentive respondents (see below). After these exclusions, 42,756 participants from 61 societies (59% female, Mage = 32.92, SDage = 14.62) were included in the analysis. Full demographic information is provided in Table S1.

We first excluded testing data.

Then, following our pre-registered criteria, we excluded participants who (i) reported to be younger than 18 years old; (ii) did not pass at least one of two attention check questions (i.e., "To verify that you are a genuine participant, please select 7" and "To verify that you are a genuine participant, please select 10%"); (iii) selected the same response options (i.e., straight-lined pattern) on two instruments with reverse-coded items that only used for attention check and not included in data analysis: six items from the disease avoidance subscale of the Fundamental Social Motives Inventory (1) and sixteen items generated for this study assessing knowledge of germ theory); (iv) retained only the first response and excluded any subsequent responses from participants who submitted more than one response (identified by account ID or student ID); (v) selected "Yes" to the question "Do you want to withdraw your consent and delete your data?".

We pre-registered a plan to exclude participants who provided implausible responses to two open-ended questions regarding height and weight estimates of the imagined target in this study. We departed from this plan because (1) many participants wrote feedback at the end of the survey indicating that height and weight were difficult to estimate, especially for those picturing a stranger, and (2) participants provided data in many different formats that could all be feasible responses for the same height estimate (e.g., 6'1", 185, 1.85, and 73). Hence, we concluded that target height and weight estimates had poor validity for screening purposes.

S1.2. Procedure and measures

The study follows the sequence outlined below. Participants were first asked to imagine a target. Then, with that target in mind, they then: (1) indicated whether a typical greeting with the target would involve physical contact, (2) reported how comfortable they would feel engaging in multiple acts of indirect contact that risk some microbe transmission from the target to themselves, and (3) completed a welfare trade-off task. The details of these procedures are described below.

S1.2.1. Target assignment

Participants were randomly assigned to one of the following targets: (i) their closest friend, (ii) an acquaintance, (iii) a stranger (an unknown person from the same society), or (iv) a person they know personally and dislike intensely (for brevity, referred to as "enemy" below). This approach was used to facilitate variation in target interpersonal value within society and mitigate potential inconsistencies in the nature of targets pictured across societies. We balanced target sex by assigning participants to picture either a female (e.g., "their closest female friend") or a male (e.g., "a male acquaintance") target in each condition. Below are the descriptions provided to participants.

Closest friend: Next, we will ask you to make some financial decisions concerning your closest male (female) friend. Please imagine a male (female) friend who is very close to you but isn't a family member or romantic partner. We will refer to this man (woman) as Person X. Before making these decisions, we will ask you to answer a few questions about Person X. Please take a moment to think about Person X and your relationship with Person X.

Acquaintance: Next, we will ask you to make some financial decisions concerning a male (female) acquaintance of yours. Please imagine a male (female) acquaintance -someone whose name you know but you do not have a close relationship with. We will refer to this man (woman) as Person X. Before making these decisions, we will ask you to answer a few questions about Person X. Please take a moment to think about Person X and your relationship with Person X.

Stranger: Next, we will ask you to make some financial decisions concerning a man (woman) from [participant's own society, e.g., the US] whom you don't know and probably won't meet in the near future. We will refer to this man (woman) as Person X. Before making these decisions, we will ask you to answer a few questions about Person X. Please take a moment to think about Person X.

Enemy: Next, we will ask you to make some financial decisions concerning a man (woman) that you know personally and dislike intensely. We will refer to this man (woman) as Person X. Before making these decisions, we will ask you to answer a few questions about Person X. Please take a moment to think about Person X and your relationship with Person X.

To encourage participants to think about the target, we asked them the following questions:

How long have you known Person X?  About how tall is Person X? (In inches/cm)  About how much does Person X weigh? (In pounds/kg)  In the past month, how many days were you in the same room as Person X?  In the past month, how many days did you have any contact with Person X? (Including inperson talking, phone calls, messages, social media, and other methods) S1.2.2. Individual-level measures Contact greeting. Participants reported whether they would typically physically contact the target during a greeting: "People often greet each other. Some greetings involve physical contact. Examples include handshakes, hugs, and kisses. Other greetings do not involve physical contact. Examples include just saying hello, using a hand gesture, or bowing. Imagine that you greeted Person X today. Would you physically touch Person X?". Participants who indicated yes were asked to select which body parts they would touch during the greeting, including back, legs, arms, hands, chest, cheeks, and lips (i.e., "Which of your body parts would touch Person X when you greet him/her?"). Responses were coded as 0 (no) and 1 (yes). Contact comfort. Participants rated their comfort with five actions involving exposure to others' microbes on a 7-point scale ranging from 1 (very uncomfortable) to 7 (very comfortable):  Sitting close enough to Person X that your legs are touching.  Standing close enough to Person X that his/her saliva might splash onto your face.  Using the same toilet seat that Person X used minutes earlier.  Putting Person X's slippers on your feet.  Drinking from the same water bottle as Person X.

The items above were developed based on a pilot study conducted in four countries, including the United States (N = 220), Portugal (N = 219), China (N = 364), and the Netherlands (N = 221). These five items were selected from an initial pool of 17 items administered in the pilot based on exploratory factor analysis and measurement invariance analysis. Further details are reported in the item selection document on OSF (https://osf.io/326xu/files/cvmnk).

Welfare trade-off ratio (WTR).

Participants completed a 15-item welfare trade-off task previously used in research on culturally diverse populations, which provides an estimate of the ratio of how much an individual values another's welfare (e.g., money) relative to their own (2, 3). In this task, participants make a series of 15 hypothetical financial decisions, choosing between an otherbenefiting option (i.e., the target gets money) and a self-benefiting option (i.e., the participant gets money). In each trial, the amounts for the other-benefiting option were fixed. The amounts for the self-benefiting option were different, and the sequence of the items was randomized. Details of each option were provided in the codebook document on the OSF: https://osf.io/326xu/files/fythp).

WTR was estimated using the following procedure. For participants who switched once from choosing the self-benefiting option to the other-benefiting option, the estimation of WTR followed two steps below: first, calculate the ratio of the amounts of self-benefiting and other-benefiting; and second, WTR was assigned to the point at which participants switched from consistently selecting self-benefiting to other-benefiting. If participants always chose the self-benefiting option, WTR was estimated as -.45; if they always chose the other-benefiting option, WTR was estimated as 1.55. If participants had more than one switch point, WTR was estimated using a consistency maximization method, and see further information for this method in the work by Delton and colleagues (2). In line with previous work, participants who reported more than two switch points in this task were treated as missing data (4).

To make the meaning of the monetary units comparable across societies, we set the amounts in other-benefiting options to the society's median per-day wage, and we calibrated the selfbenefiting amounts accordingly. Full amounts for each society are provided in the codebook document on the OSF: https://osf.io/326xu/files/fythp). Below are all 15 items used in the U.S. sample as an example. Items are identical across societies, except for the monetary amounts.

Which of the following would you choose? Option 1: You get $334, Person X gets $0. Option 2: You get $0, Person X gets $230. Which of the following would you choose? Option 1: You get $288, Person X gets $0. Option 2: You get $0, Person X gets $230. Which of the following would you choose? Option 1: You get $242, Person X gets $0. Option 2: You get $0, Person X gets $230. Which of the following would you choose? Option 1: You get $127, Person X gets $0. Option 2: You get $0, Person X gets $230. Which of the following would you choose? Option 1: You get $104, Person X gets $0. Option 2: You get $0, Person X gets $230. Which of the following would you choose? S1.2.3. Society-level measures

Historical pathogen prevalence. Murray and Schaller developed an index of historical pathogen prevalence, which we employed in our analysis (5). This index assesses the presence of nine diseases within 230 geopolitical regions across history based on epidemiological atlases, including leishmaniasis, schistosomes, trypanosomes, leprosy, malaria, typhus, filariae, dengue, and tuberculosis. Positive values indicate a higher-than-average disease prevalence; the greater the value, the higher the prevalence. Scores were available for all 61 societies in our dataset.

Cultural factors. We employed three cultural indices: individualism-collectivism (larger values indicate more individualism and less collectivism) (6), tightness-looseness (greater values indicate more tightness) (7, 8), and relational mobility (larger values indicate greater mobility in relationships) (9). Data for these indices were available for 58, 41, and 29 societies in our dataset, respectively.

Contemporary pathogen prevalence.

We used two indices to represent contemporary pathogen prevalence. The first was the index developed by Fincher et al. (2008), which was constructed from contemporary epidemiological data obtained from the Global Infectious Diseases and Epidemiology Online Network (GIDEON). The index covers 22 infectious diseases across seven pathogen categories (i.e., leishmaniasis, trypanosomes, malaria, schistosomes, filariae, spirochetes, and leprosy). Each disease was coded on a three-point prevalence scale, and scores were summed to create a composite index of contemporary pathogen prevalence (referred to as the contemporary pathogen prevalence index below). The second index used WHO infectious-disease data, following prior parasite-stress research that has relied on similar indicators to capture contemporary pathogen burden (10). We used age-standardized mortality rates from infectious and parasitic diseases (per 100,000 population) from the WHO Mortality Database. Whereas earlier studies were based on a single year, we averaged the death rate across all available years to reduce annual fluctuations (referred to as the average death rate below). We excluded post-2019 observations to minimize potential bias introduced by the COVID-19 pandemic. Data for these two indices were available for 55 and 45 societies in our dataset, respectively. The bivariate correlations of these two indices with the historical pathogen prevalence in the current sample were 0.68 and 0.44 (both ps < 0.001), respectively.

S2. Analytic strategy

S2.1. Reliability, validity, and measurement invariance for contact comfort Reliability of contact comfort within each society was assessed using Cronbach's alpha. The convergent validity of the contact comfort measure was assessed using multilevel models that examined its associations with two pathogen-avoidance measures: pathogen disgust sensitivity (11) and the disease-avoidance subscale of the Fundamental Social Motives Inventory (1). Next, measurement invariance across the two data recruitment categories (a panel company and collaborating universities) was assessed by multi𝜏group confirmatory factor analysis of contact comfort using the lavaan package in R (12-14).

S2.2. Within-society analys e s and meta-analyses of infection-risky social contact

For each society, we first calculated the means (M) and standard deviations (SD) of contact comfort, contact greeting, and WTR. Next, we examined the bivariate correlations between WTR and both contact comfort (Pearson's r) and between WTR and contact greeting (Point-biserial r).

To quantify the variation in these correlations across societies, we applied Fisher's z transformation to the correlation coefficients to approximate normality. We then performed a twolevel meta-analysis of the society-specific correlations using restricted maximum likelihood (REML) via the R package metafor (15). The model estimated the weighted average correlation and the between-society heterogeneity (𝜏 2 ). For interpretation, the average correlation and its confidence interval were backtransformed from Fisher's z to Pearson's r.

S2.3. Between-society analysis of infection-risky social contact and WTR

To account for the nested structure of data, we employed multilevel modeling (16) and used the lme4 (17) and the lmerTest (18) packages in R (version 4.5.0). To estimate the intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC), we fitted intercept-only multilevel models (null models) -specifying random intercepts for societies -for contact comfort, contact greeting, and WTR. We also assessed variation in WTR across relationship categories and the variance in WTR explained by relationship category.

For the main analysis for contact comfort, we first analyzed the association between contact comfort and WTR when accounting for relationship category. We controlled for sample (panel vs university), target sex, participant sex, and the interaction between target sex and participant sex. The decision to include a random slope for WTR was based on a comparison of model fit indices between models with and without the random slope, including the likelihood ratio test, the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), and the Akaike information criterion (AIC) (19). Specifically, the random slope was retained when the likelihood-ratio test for the nested models was significant (p < 0.05), which tests whether the added variance component differs from zero. AIC and BIC (smaller values preferred) were reported to assess parsimony and predictive adequacy.

Next, we fitted separate models to examine whether each level-2 predictor (i.e., historical pathogen prevalence, individualism-collectivism, tightness, and relational mobility) was associated with infection-risky contact. We accounted for relationship factors (i.e., WTR and relationship category) and controlled for the same variables as described above. The R package PartR2 was used to estimate semi-partial R² (20).

We then tested the moderations of societal-level predictors on the association between infectionrisky contact and WTR. We fitted separate models testing the interaction between WTR and each level-2 predictor, including historical pathogen prevalence and three cultural factors (i.e., individualism-collectivism, tightness, and relational mobility). All level-2 predictors were standardized. We then tested the two-way interactions between each level-2 predictor and WTR.

We also tested whether societal-level factors moderate the association between WTR and infection-risky contact within relationship category.

We analyzed contact greeting using the same process with generalized multilevel models. The R packages interactions (21) and emmeans (22) were used for simple slope analysis and Tukey's post hoc test.

S2.4. Analyzing associations between infection-risky social contact and relationship category

As a complementary analysis of interpersonal value, we examined whether closer relationships were associated with greater comfort with infection-risky contact and a higher likelihood of physical touching during greetings, both within and across societies. For the within-society analysis, we estimated descriptive means of both outcomes for each relationship category. For the across-society analysis, we first regressed both outcomes on dummy-coded relationship category, controlling for the same variables described above (sample source, participant sex, and target sex). We then fitted separate models testing the interaction between relationship category and each societal-level predictor (i.e., historical pathogen prevalence, individualism, tightness, and relational mobility).

S2.5. Control for geographic and cultural nonindependence

To test the robustness of results after controlling for societal non-independence, we fitted Bayesian multilevel models via the brm package (23). Following Claessens and colleagues (24), spatial non-independence was controlled by adding a Gaussian process over the latitude and longitude of the geographic center within each society. Cultural non-independence was accounted for by adding a random intercept for society with a covariance matrix based on a linguistic matrix, which was obtained from the work by Claessens and colleagues (24). These methods allow societies to covary according to geographic and/or linguistic similarities. For models examining contact comfort, both geographic and linguistic nonindependence were included. Due to convergence issues, we fitted separate models with geographic proximity or linguistic proximity for models examining contact greeting.

S2.6. Analyzing the association between infection-risky social contact and contemporary pathogen prevalence

To explore the influence of contemporary pathogen prevalence on infection-risky social contact, we also assessed (i) whether greater contemporary pathogen prevalence was associated with lower contact comfort and a lower likelihood of contact during greetings, and (ii) whether it moderated the associations of WTR and relationship category with infection-risky contact. The analyses followed the same analytical steps used for historical pathogen prevalence.

S3. Supplementary results

S3. Supplementary results

S3.1. Reliability, validity, and measurement invariance for contact comfort

The results suggested good reliability across all societies (alpha coefficients ranging from 0.81 to 0.90; see Table S2). Greater contact comfort was associated with both lower pathogen disgust sensitivity (b = -0.24, 95% CI [-0.26, -0.21], p < 0.001) and disease avoidance (b = -0.19, 95% CI [-0.21, -0.17], p < 0.001). These findings were consistent with theoretical predictions regarding pathogen-avoidance constructs, providing evidence for the convergent validity of the contact comfort measure. Contact comfort had acceptable levels of configural invariance (all CFI changes across models smaller than 0.01; Table S3).

S3.2 . Meta-analysis of within-society associations

In both outcomes, a majority of the observed variance reflected true effect heterogeneity rather than sampling error (contact comfort: I² = 67.19%; contact greeting: I² = 61.75%). Full results of correlation coefficients for each society are in Table S4.

S3.3. Variation in WTR across societies and relationship categories Between-society differences accounted for about 2% of the variation in WTR (ICC = 0.02), suggesting minimal variation in overall WTR (25, 26). As expected, WTR varied across the target's relationship category, F(3, 35695) = 2093, p < 0.001. WTR was highest for friends (M = 0.55), followed by acquaintances (M = 0.29), strangers (M = 0.18), and enemies (M = -0.05). All pairwise comparisons are statistically significant, all ps < 0.001. Relationship category accounted for approximately 15% of the variance in WTR (semi-partial R² = 0.15).

S3.4. Variation in contact comfort and contact greeting across relationship categories Across societies, contact comfort and contact greeting varied across relationship categories, F(3, 42317) = 3654.16, p < 0.001, and 𝜏 2 (3) = 3937.47, p < 0.001, respectively. Specifically, individuals reported greater comfort and a higher likelihood of physical contact during greetings with friends, followed by acquaintances, strangers, and enemies (all pairwise comparisons are statistically significant, ps < 0.001; Tables S8 and S12). Such a pattern was consistent within most societies (Fig. S3). Across all relationship categories, the hands are the most common area of contact (Fig. S4). The arms are also common areas of contact, particularly when greeting friends and acquaintances. In contrast, lips and legs are uncommon during greetings across all four relationship categories.

S3.5. Interactions between relationship category and historical pathogen prevalence on infectionrisky contact

The interaction between relationship category and historical pathogen prevalence on contact comfort was statistically significant, F(3, 51) = 3.61, p = 0.019. Specifically, relative to friends, the negative association between historical pathogen prevalence and contact comfort was significantly attenuated for strangers (b = 0.20, 95% CI [0.07, 0.34], p = 0.003; Table S14) and enemies (b = 0.19, 95% CI [0.06, 0.32], p = 0.004), whereas no significant difference was observed between acquaintances (b = 0.10, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.21], p = 0.067) and friends. As displayed in Fig. S5A, simple slopes showed that the decline in contact comfort was strongest for friends. Similarly, contact comfort was greater for friends and acquaintances in societies with lower historical pathogen prevalence, whereas no differences were observed for strangers or enemies across levels of historical pathogen prevalence (Table S15). These findings are consistent with the results from Bayesian models with a control for societal non-independence. The simple slopes of historical pathogen prevalence were credibly negative for friends (b = -0.23, 95% HPD [-0.39, -0.07]) and acquaintances (b = -0.13, 95% HPD [-0.25, -0.001]), whereas the slopes for strangers (b = -0.02, 95% HPD [-0.14, 0.10]) and enemies (b = -0.04, 95% HPD [-0.17, 0.09]) were not credibly different from zero. Results of interaction effects and pairwise comparison of Bayesian models are reported in Tables S16 and S17, respectively.

The interaction between relationship category and historical pathogen prevalence on contact greeting was also statistically significant, 𝜏 2 (3) = 13.12, p = 0.004. Relative to friends, the association between historical pathogen prevalence and contact greeting was significantly more positive for enemies (OR = 1.28, 95% CI [1.08, 1.50], p = 0.003), whereas neither acquaintances (OR = 1.10, 95% CI [0.99, 1.23], p = 0.086) nor strangers (OR = 1.05, 95% CI [0.90, 1.22], p = 0.545) differed significantly from friends (Table S18). Simple slopes showed that historical pathogen prevalence was positively associated with contact greeting for enemies, but was not significantly associated with greeting for friends, acquaintances, or strangers (Fig. S5B). Pairwise comparisons across levels of historical pathogen prevalence within each relationship category were not statistically significant, all ps > 0.05 (Table S19). In Bayesian models with a control for societal non-independence, the simple slopes were not credibly different from zero for any relationship category, including enemies (b = 0.19, 95% HPD [-0.02, 0.41]), as well as friends (b = -0.06, 95% HPD [-0.29, 0.19]), acquaintances (b = 0.04, 95% HPD [-0.20, 0.27]), and strangers (b = -0.01, 95% HPD [-0.22, 0.21]). Results of interaction effects and pairwise comparison of Bayesian models are reported in Tables S20 and S21, respectively.

Overall, these results indicate that historical pathogen prevalence is associated with infectionrisky contact primarily in relatively high-value relationships, whereas in low-value relationships, pathogen prevalence showed unrobust associations.

S3.6. Interactions between relationship category and cultural factors on infection-risky contact

Cultural factors also moderated the association between relationship category and both contact comfort and contact greeting. For contact comfort, the interaction between relationship category and individualism was significant, F(3, 48) = 6.13, p = 0.001 (see details in Table S28). Specifically, relative to friends, the association was significantly attenuated for acquaintances (b = -0.10, 95% CI [-0.17, -0.03], p = 0.005), strangers (b = -0.19, 95% CI [-0.28, -0.10], p < 0.001), and enemies (b = -0.17, 95% CI [-0.25, -0.08], p < 0.001). Simple slope analysis showed that contact comfort was positively associated with individualism for friends and acquaintances but not for strangers or enemies (Fig. S6). Similarly, contact comfort was greater in more individualistic societies for friends and acquaintances, whereas no differences emerged for strangers or enemies (Table S29). The interaction between relationship category and tightness was also significant, F(3, 43) = 6.31, p = 0.001. Contact comfort was less negatively associated with tightness for acquaintances (b = 0.09, 95% CI [0.02, 0.16], p = 0.011) and enemies (b = 0.16, 95% CI [0.07, 0.25], p < 0.001), but not for strangers (b = 0.10, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.21], p = 0.085), relative to friends. However, none of the simple slopes were statistically significant (Fig. S6), and contact comfort did not differ across levels of tightness for any relationship category (Table S29).

The interaction between relationship category and relational mobility was also significant, F(3, 23) = 6.33, p = 0.003. Relative to friends, the association was attenuated for acquaintances (b = -0.17, 95% CI [-0.26, -0.07], p = 0.001), strangers (b = -0.25, 95% CI [-0.38, -0.13], p < 0.001), and enemies (b = -0.21, 95% CI [-0.31, -0.11], p < 0.001). Simple slope analysis suggested that contact comfort was positively associated with relational mobility for friends, acquaintances, and enemies, but not for strangers (Fig. S6). Similarly, contact comfort was greater in societies with higher relational mobility for all relationship categories except strangers (Table S29). Results were largely consistent in Bayesian models with a control for societal non-independence, except that the simple slopes of individualism for acquaintances and of relational mobility for enemies were not credibly different from zero (Fig. S6; Tables S30 and S31).

For contact greeting, the interaction between relationship category and individualism was significant, 𝜏 2 (3) = 10.87, p = 0.012 (see details in Table S34). Relative to friends, the association was attenuated for enemies (OR = 0.82, 95% CI [0.73, 0.93], p = 0.001), but not for acquaintances (OR = 0.93, 95% CI [0.86, 1.00], p = 0.054) or strangers (OR = 0.91, 95% CI [0.81, 1.02], p = 0.094). None of the simple slopes were statistically significant (Fig. S6), and contact greeting did not differ across levels of individualism for any relationship category (Table S35). The interaction between relationship category and tightness was also significant, 𝜏 2 (3) = 14.63, p = 0.002 (see details in Table S34). As with individualism, only the association between tightness and contact greeting for enemies differed significantly from that for friends (OR = 1.23, 95% CI [1.09, 1.38], p = 0.001), whereas the associations for acquaintances (OR = 1.06, 95% CI [0.97, 1.16], p = 0.207) and strangers (OR = 1.07, 95% CI [0.95, 1.21], p = 0.238) did not differ significantly from that for friends. Simple slope analysis indicated that contact greeting was negatively associated with tightness for friends and strangers, but not for acquaintances or enemies (Fig. S6). No statistically significant differences emerged in pairwise comparisons across levels of tightness using Tukey adjustment, all ps > 0.05 (Table S35). The interaction between relationship category and relational mobility was likewise statistically significant, 𝜏 2 (3) = 15, p = 0.002 (see details in Table S34). Relative to friends, the association was attenuated for strangers (OR = 0.82, 95% CI [0.72, 0.93], p = 0.002) and enemies (OR = 0.81, 95% CI [0.70, 0.95], p = 0.010), but not for acquaintances (OR = 1.02, 95% CI [0.91, 1.14], p = 0.731). Contact greeting was positively associated with relational mobility for all four relationship categories (Fig. S6) and was correspondingly more likely in societies with higher relational mobility across all relationship categories (Table S35). Results were largely consistent in Bayesian models with a control for societal non-independence, except that the simple slopes of tightness for friends and strangers, and of relational mobility for strangers and enemies, were no longer credibly different from zero (Fig. S6; Tables S36 and S37).

In sum, cultural factors primarily influenced the willingness to engage in infection-risky contact with relatively close relationship partners. Individualism was associated with greater contact comfort only toward friends, whereas relational mobility was associated with greater contact comfort and a higher likelihood of contact greetings with friends and acquaintances. Tightness did not show reliable associations with either outcome. Similar to historical pathogen prevalence, cultural factors showed little evidence of consistently shaping infection-risky contact with relatively low-value relationships.

S3.7. The association between infection-risky contact and WTR within relationship category

When accounting for relationship category, the interaction between historical pathogen prevalence and WTR was not statistically significant for contact comfort (b = -0.06, 95% CI [-0.11, 0.004], p = 0.07). This interaction was statistically significant for contact greeting (OR = 0.87, 95% CI [0.81, 0.94], p < 0.001), and it remained negative in Bayesian models accounting for societal non-independence (ORMedian = 0.87, 95% CrI [0.80, 0.94]). However, Johnson-Neyman analyses of frequentist models indicated that the simple effect of historical pathogen prevalence was statistically significant (p < 0.05) only when WTR is below -0.72 or above 3.15 -values outside the observed range of WTR (minimum: -0.45, maximum: 1.55; Fig. S7A). Consistent with this, the 95% credible intervals for all simple slopes at the tested levels of WTR included 1 in the Bayesian analyses.

The interaction between interpersonal value and individualism was statistically significant for contact greeting (OR = 1.11, 95% CI [1.05, 1.17], p < 0.001) and it remained positive in Bayesian models accounting for societal non-independence (ORMedian = 1.11, 95% CrI [1.05, 1.17]), though the simple slopes of individualism were statistically significant only at values of WTR below -1.09 or above 2.46, outside the observed range (Fig. S7B). The 95% credible intervals for all simple slopes in the Bayesian analyses also included 1.

Relational mobility moderated the association between WTR and contact comfort (b = 0.06, 95% CI [0.01, 0.11], p < 0.05), and it remained positive in Bayesian models accounting for societal nonindependence (bMedian = 0.06, 95% CrI [0.01, 0.11]). Simple slopes of relational mobility were statistically significant across the observed range of WTR in the frequentist analyses. However, in the Bayesian analyses, the 95% credible interval for the simple slope at the lowest observed WTR included zero (Fig. S7C).

The interactions between tightness and WTR on both outcomes (contact comfort: b = -0.04, 95% CI [-0.08, 0.01], p = 0.152; contact greeting: OR = 0.97, 95% CI [0.93, 1.03], p = 0.356) were not statistically significant.

Overall, when accounting for relationship category, relational mobility consistently moderated the association between WTR and contact comfort, indicating that even within the same relationship category, people in societies with higher relational mobility were more comfortable engaging in infection-risky physical contact with individuals they valued more highly. By contrast, the moderating effects of historical pathogen prevalence and individualism reached statistical significance only outside the observed range of WTR.

S3.8. The association between infection-risky contact and contemporary pathogen prevalence

In Bayesian multilevel models with a control for societal non-independence, the associations of the contemporary pathogen prevalence index with contact comfort (bMedian = -0.02, 95% CrI [-0.10, 0.05]; Table S42) and contact greeting (ORMedian = 1.09, 95% CrI [0.96, 1.28]; Table S45) were not credibly different from zero.

The interaction between the contemporary pathogen prevalence index and WTR was credible for both contact comfort (bMedian = -0.07, 95% CrI [-0.12, -0.02]; Table S42) and contact greeting (ORMedian = 0.87, 95% CrI [0.82, 0.93]; Table S45). For contact comfort, simple slope analysis indicated that contemporary pathogen prevalence was credibly negatively associated with contact comfort at higher levels of WTR (WTR at 1.55: bMedian = -0.13, 95% HPD [-0.24, -0.02]; WTR at 1: bMedian = -0.09, 95% HPD [-0.18, -0.004]), whereas the slopes at lower levels of WTR were not credibly different from zero. For contact greeting, the association was credibly positive at the lowest level of WTR (WTR at -0.45: ORMedian = 1.16, 95% HPD [1.05, 1.28]), whereas the slopes at the remaining levels were not credibly different from zero. By contrast, for both outcomes the positive association between WTR and contact was credible at all levels of contemporary pathogen prevalence but declined as prevalence increased (contact comfort: at - 1 SD, bMedian = 1.20, 95% HPD [1.12, 1.28]; mean, bMedian = 1.13, 95% HPD [1.08, 1.19]; +1 SD, bMedian = 1.06, 95% HPD [0.99, 1.14]; contact greeting: at -1 SD, ORMedian = 3.05, 95% HPD [2.80, 3.38]; mean, ORMedian = 2.67, 95% HPD [2.51, 2.85]; +1 SD, ORMedian = 2.33, 95% HPD [2.15, 2.54]).

The interaction between the contemporary pathogen prevalence index and relationship category was credible for contact comfort (Table S42): relative to friends, the association was credibly less negative for acquaintances (bMedian = 0.09, 95% CrI [0.01, 0.18], pd = 98.5%), strangers (bMedian = 0.13, 95% CrI [0.03, 0.24], pd = 99.3%), and enemies (bMedian = 0.14, 95% CrI [0.04, 0.23], pd = 99.6%). Simple slope analysis showed that contemporary pathogen prevalence was credibly negatively associated with contact comfort for friends (bMedian = -0.13, 95% HPD [-0.24, -0.02]) but not for the other relationship categories, and contact comfort was credibly greater in societies with lower contemporary pathogen prevalence for friends only (Table S44). For contact greeting, relative to friends, the association was credibly more positive for acquaintances (ORMedian = 1.13, 95% CrI [1.03, 1.22], pd = 99.6%; Table S45), whereas the differences for strangers and enemies were not credible. None of the simple slopes of the contemporary pathogen prevalence index were credibly different from zero, and no credible differences emerged in the pairwise comparisons for any relationship category (Table S47).

All other estimates for the contemporary pathogen prevalence index were not credibly different from zero (Tables S42-S47). For average death rate, no credible associations with either contact comfort or contact greeting emerged in any model, whether as a main effect, in interaction with WTR, or in interaction with relationship category; none of the simple slopes or pairwise comparisons were credibly different from zero (Tables S43, S44, S46, and S47).

Overall, consistent with the historical measure of pathogen prevalence, these findings suggest that greater contemporary pathogen prevalence might be associated with reduced willingness to engage in infection-risky contact with high-value social partners. Yet these interpretations should be made with caution, as a parallel index of contemporary pathogen threat, average death rate, showed no credible associations with either outcome. Fig.S1. Figure 1.

Figure 1. Cross-societal variation in contact comfort and contact greeting (A) Estimated society-level means for contact comfort, measured as the average of five items assessing contact comfort. (B) Estimated society-level probabilities of individuals engaging in physical contact during greetings. Higher scores indicate greater comfort with these behaviors and a higher likelihood of physical contact during greetings. Points represent society-level

Figure 2.

Figure 2. Interpersonal value positively associates with social contact across societies (A and C) Associations between welfare trade-off ratio (WTR) and contact comfort (A) and contact greeting (C). Higher scores on the y-axis indicate greater comfort with these behaviors and a higher likelihood of physical contact during greetings. Greater WTR reflects placing greater value on others' welfare relative to one's own. Black lines show the overall effect across societies, and colored lines show effects within each society. (B and D) Maps of Pearson correlation coefficients for contact comfort (B) and contact greeting (D). Darker color indicates stronger positive correlations.

Fig S2.

Fig.S2. Simple slopes of cultural factors on infection-risky contact at four levels of WTR (1.55, 1, 0, and -0.45) (A -C) Predicted contact comfort as a function of individualism (A), tightness (B), and relational mobility at four levels of WTR. (D -F) Predicted contact greeting as a function of individualism (D), tightness (E), and relational mobility (F) at four levels of WTR. Lines represent simple slopes at four levels of WTR: 1.55 indicates the highest value of WTR possible in the study, 1 indicates target welfare valued equally to one's own, 0 indicates indifference to the target's welfare, and -0.45 indicates the lowest value of WTR possible in the study. Lines represent frequentist simple slopes. Text in the upper-left reports frequentist estimates of simple slopes, 95% confidence intervals (shown as shaded regions), and p-values, as well as Bayesian estimates of simple slopes and 95% credible intervals.
